# Measured results

No accuracy or performance numbers are claimed for kore-self on real data.
A number may be quoted elsewhere only if it has a row here with: n, baseline, interval, date, commit.

**Every number below comes from synthetic data** generated by `kore-self/src/synth.rs`
(Poisson topic counts, uniform and planted-probability actions, phrases written by the
same author as the detectors). They show how the rule-based detectors behave on data
that matches their assumptions. They are not real-life accuracy, and real logs will
be burstier, messier and phrased differently.

## How to reproduce

```
cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_learning --offline --release
cargo test -p kore-self --offline        # includes measured_detector_quality_on_synthetic_data_stays_above_floor
```

Seeds 1..=20, noise 0.0 / 0.2 / 0.5, default parameters
`{"habit_min_n":8,"habit_lb":0.5,"habit_window_days":0,"change_llr":12.0,"change_min_seg":10,"change_min_ratio":1.8,"change_min_total":10,"habit_lift":0.0,"habit_max_share":0.9}` (the two lift parameters were added after the tagged table was first recorded; the tagged table is unchanged by them, see "Tagged lives after the fix").
Each synthetic life is 150 days from 2024-01-01 with about 2000-3000 events. Noise adds
that fraction of extra events: 40% random actions inside the habit contexts (which
dilutes the habits), 40% random topic mentions (which flattens topic shifts), 20% chatter,
including near-miss phrases ("They now prefer coffee for work.", "I prefer tea for
mornings.", "If I now prefer ...").

Actual output of the run (median [min-max] over the 20 seeds):

## Definitions

* Habit truth: planted (context, action) with probability >= 0.6 (three per life: 0.9, 0.8, 0.7).
  Non-habit contexts: one weak planted action (p = 0.35) and two uniform contexts.
  Habit recall falls with noise because the injected random actions pull a planted
  rate such as 0.7 toward the 0.5 bound; that is the detector refusing to call it a habit, and
  it is the main behaviour the evolution loop can tune (lower `habit_lb`).
* Change point match: same topic and detected day within 7 days of the planted day.
  Precision = matched detections / all detections; recall = matched planted changes / planted changes.
  Delay is measured by re-running the detector on the data truncated day by day.
* Stance: event-level. The cited event must be a planted statement; key accuracy checks the topic.
  The distractor phrases and the matcher were written by the same author, so 1.00 says the matcher
  follows its own grammar, not that it understands real writing.
* min-n refusal: the share of planted tiny contexts that were refused.

## Test floors

The test `measured_detector_quality_on_synthetic_data_stays_above_floor` (in
`kore-self/src/learn_tests.rs`) fails if a run drops below slightly under the floor measured
above: habit precision >= 0.95; stance precision, recall and key accuracy >= 0.95; min-n
refusal >= 0.95; change precision >= 0.45, recall >= 0.6, per-seed FP rate <= 0.25, date
error <= 5 days; habit recall >= 0.95 (0% noise), >= 0.6 (20%), median >= 0.3 (50%).
These thresholds guard against regressions on synthetic data; they are not accuracy claims.

## Evolution loop: one example, not a measurement

`self_evolve_rules` on the end-to-end test's synthetic life (seed 11, 20% noise, 150 days, cut date
2024-04-14, 4 selection origins, 5 evaluation origins, horizon 14 days, margin 0.02) proposed
`habit_lb` 0.5 -> 0.4 (13 candidates tried). Next-period habit F1 on the evaluation origins:
candidate 0.929, incumbent 0.870, trivial baseline 0.491; verdict promoted
(code at commit f8440c8a; see README "Learning quick start"). This is one run on
one synthetic life and says nothing about other data. Whether the loop helps across seeds has
not been measured.

## Free-text lives with keyword rules (synthetic, author-written templates)

Same detectors, same 20 seeds, same noise levels and parameters, but the synthetic life is
written as short journal sentences with no tags (`synth::free_text_config`) and read
through the keyword rules `synth::free_text_rules()` (the same format as a user's
`tag_rules.txt`). **The sentence templates, the distractors and the keyword rules were all written by
the same author, in one sitting, knowing each other.** The numbers say how the rule layer behaves on text that was
written to be mostly matchable, with these deliberate difficulties: varied phrasing
(3-4 templates per context, action and topic); 40% of the occasions that did not take
a planted habit mention it negated ("did not run at all", "skipped the podcast"), 15% of those
as post-negations the guard cannot see ("the run was called off"); 10% of real actions and
topic mentions use a synonym the rules do not list ("did laps around the track");
keyword-bearing distractors in the noise ("The bus ran late again.", "My reading glasses broke.").
They are not accuracy on anyone's real journal.

How occasions are counted (code: `learn/habits.rs`, docs in `learn/tagrules.rs`): a keyword
context is an occasion for each event with a sentence matching it, and the action counts if its
keywords match in the same sentence; the built-in `weekday`/`weekend` contexts are day-level
(every day with an event; the action counts if any event of the day matches).

### What was wrong at first, and the fix

The first version of this section (commit 5d45ece3) reported overall habit precision 0.50 / 0.29 / 0.00 (median at 0 / 20 / 50% noise),
with 1 to 12 false habits per life in the built-in `weekday` / `weekend` contexts. Cause: the synthetic life has about 15 events a day
and no weekday structure, so an action such as `run` occurs on 60-70% of weekdays *and* on 60-70% of weekend days. A context that holds on
almost every unit gives every frequent action a high in-context rate, and the Wilson bound alone cannot tell "the action's base rate"
from "a habit of this context". (An even earlier variant that treated keyword contexts day-level too gave mean precision 0.21 at 0% noise
for the same reason and was replaced by sentence-level occasions.)

The fix (`habits::detect_full`, parameters in the rule set, see README "Free-text journals"):

1. **Lift test** (`habit_lift`, default 0.0): the in-context Wilson lower bound must exceed the Wilson upper bound of the same action's
   rate in all *other* contexts of the same family (stored tags, built-in date contexts, keyword contexts) plus the margin. For weekday the
   comparison is exactly the weekend. A negative value switches the test off. With fewer than `habit_min_n` out-of-context occasions the
   test cannot be made and the habit is kept (a log with a single context has nothing to compare with).
2. **Uninformative contexts** (`habit_max_share`, default 0.9): a rule-derived context that holds on more than this share of its units
   (days for weekday/weekend, events for keyword contexts) is dropped and reported (`uninformative_contexts` in `self_learn`).
3. Min-n refusal is unchanged and comes first.

The defaults are the principled values (a margin of zero, the 90% suggested in advance), not fitted. Parameter choices were looked at on
tuning seeds 101..120 only (never on the reported seeds 1..20): on those seeds the free-text overall habit precision was median 1.00 with
per-seed minimum 0.75 / 0.67 / 0.00 at 0 / 20 / 50% noise (0.00 where nothing planted was detected and one false habit existed), and a median of 0
built-in-context habits per life (maximum 1). So a residual false habit does occur on some lives; on the reported seeds none did.

Before the fix (same seeds): overall habit precision 0.50 / 0.29 / 0.00 and 2 / 5 / 9 built-in-context habits per life (medians); everything else in the table is
identical before and after (habit recall, change columns, stance columns), so the fix removed false habits without costing planted-habit recall on these data.

Reading the table honestly:

* Overall habit precision is now 1.00 at every seed. Caveats: (a) at 50% noise most lives detect no planted habit at all (recall 0.07), and the harness
  prints a precision of "nothing detected" as 1.00, so that cell is vacuous; (b) the tuning seeds showed that false habits do not vanish entirely
  (see above); (c) the planted contexts were never at risk from the lift test here because the other contexts use different actions, so these data do not show
  what the lift test costs when a true habit shares its action with other contexts (it would be refused, by design).
* Habit recall (planted habits found, 3 per life) is unchanged and falls with noise like the tagged table, plus loss from unlisted synonyms and unseen
  post-negations: mean 0.93 / 0.70 / 0.07 at 0 / 20 / 50% noise versus 1.00 / 0.85 / 0.43 for tagged lives. Precision recovered; recall did not improve and is still poor at 50% noise.
* Topic change detection is slightly worse than with tags (mean recall 0.92 / 0.90 / 0.88 versus 0.97 / 0.93 / 0.90; delay 8.2 / 9.1 / 10.1 days
  versus 7.7 / 7.8 / 9.1) because 10% of mentions use unlisted words. Its false-positive rate is 1 or 2 of 100 unchanged series.
* Stances never used tags, so they are unchanged (the same-author caveat above applies).

### Tagged lives after the fix

The lift test applies to stored-tag contexts too (family "stored tags"). Re-measured on seeds 1..20 the tagged table printed above in this file is identical to the
table before the change in every cell (habit precision 1.00 [1.00-1.00], recall 1.00 / 0.85 / 0.43 means, and the rest): in these lives each planted habit's action is
rare in the other contexts, so the lift test refuses nothing. Existing tagged revisions are not rewritten (their rationale text is unchanged); only the
numbers and a new `out_of_context` field in the `self_learn` detail are added.

Test floors for this section (`free_text_measured_quality_stays_above_floor`, set slightly under the minima above):
overall and planted-context habit precision >= 0.95; at most 1 built-in-context habit per life; stance precision and recall >= 0.95; min-n refusal >= 0.95;
change precision >= 0.3 and recall >= 0.3 per seed; change false-positive rate <= 0.25; date error <= 6 days;
habit recall >= 0.6 (0% noise, per-seed minimum) and median >= 0.5 (20%). There is deliberately no floor for habit recall at 50% noise.

Not measured for free text: any real journal; synonyms or sentences written by someone other than the rule author;
`negation = all`; the evolution loop and ledger on free text beyond a functional test (they now read `tag_rules.txt`
like `self_learn`, `evolve_and_ledger_use_the_same_virtual_tags_as_learn`; their scores on free-text lives are not measured).

## Being loop: chooser in a simulated world (synthetic world, author-defined rewards)

Everything here comes from `kore-self/src/being/` (a deterministic simulated world; no real data). The tasks (arithmetic, linear equations, physics formulas, sequences), the costs, the rewards and the scripted solvers were all written by the same author. The being's "preference" for a domain is produced by those defined rewards (reward points per energy unit spent); the numbers say how well the UCB1 chooser finds the best-paying domain in this world, not anything about general ability.

Setup: 20 worlds (world seeds 1..20, the report seeds); each world has a hidden profile (reward scale, base cost, difficulty mix per domain) derived from its seed. Every policy gets the same budget of 600 energy units (about 99 steps) and the same tasks at the same step. "oracle" is told the domain with the best expected reward per energy (estimated by 3000 sampled tasks); it can still be beaten in a single world by luck. The exploration constant of the chooser (0.05) was chosen on separate tuning seeds 101..120 (c in 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.5; 0.05 gave the highest mean reward per energy there, 1.93 against an oracle of 2.12). Intervals are 95% t-intervals of the mean over the 20 worlds. Run `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release` (2026-10-24, commit 55dc05f7).

| policy | mean reward per energy unit | 95% interval of the mean | per-world range |
|---|---|---|---|
| random domain | 1.295 | [1.167, 1.424] | 0.896-1.937 |
| always arithmetic | 1.650 | [1.416, 1.883] | 0.849-2.399 |
| always algebra | 1.467 | [1.302, 1.631] | 0.866-2.240 |
| always physics | 0.627 | [0.467, 0.788] | 0.328-1.495 |
| always pattern | 1.525 | [1.325, 1.725] | 0.761-2.472 |
| oracle (hidden best domain) | 1.902 | [1.702, 2.102] | 1.102-2.472 |
| learned chooser (UCB1) | 1.694 | [1.512, 1.876] | 1.050-2.370 |

Hidden best domain over the 20 report worlds: arithmetic 10, algebra 3, physics 0, pattern 7.

| quantity (report seeds 1..20) | mean | 95% interval of the mean | range |
|---|---|---|---|
| regret per energy, learned vs oracle | 0.208 | [0.087, 0.329] | -0.115 to 0.826 |
| regret per energy, random vs oracle | 0.607 | [0.431, 0.783] | 0.087 to 1.300 |
| total reward in the budget, learned (points) | 1013 | [904, 1122] | 627-1415 |
| total reward in the budget, random (points) | 776 | [699, 854] | 537-1162 |
| share of the learned picks on the best domain, steps 1-30 | 0.49 | [0.35, 0.64] | 0.03-0.87 |
| steps 31-80 | 0.58 | [0.36, 0.79] | 0.00-1.00 |
| step 81 on | 0.50 | [0.27, 0.73] | 0.00-1.00 |
| share of random picks on the best domain | 0.25 | [0.23, 0.27] | 0.18-0.32 |

Reading: the learned chooser earns about 31% more reward per energy than random choice (1.69 against 1.30; learned beat random in 18 of 20 worlds) and closes about two thirds of the gap between random and the oracle (regret 0.21 against 0.61). It is NOT better than the best fixed domain on average: always-arithmetic scored 1.65 and the learned chooser beat it in only 8 of 20 worlds (always-algebra 11, always-pattern 10, always-physics 20 of 20). It concentrates slowly: in 12 of 20 worlds the trailing 20 picks reached 60% on the best domain at some point (median first at step 20, which is mostly the initial exploration), and the share of picks on the best domain stays near 0.5, because several domains pay almost the same and the roughly 100-step budget leaves little time to separate them. On the tuning seeds the numbers were similar (learned 1.93, random 1.36, oracle 2.12, hidden best: arithmetic 6, algebra 11, pattern 3). The claim is only: under these defined rewards the learned chooser collects more reward per energy than random choice and than always-physics, and about the same as the best single fixed domain.

Other tests (all in `kore-self/src/being/tests.rs`, `tests/e2e_being.rs`): two worlds with different hidden best domains give different preferences, and in each the preferred domain has about the best reward per energy in the being's own log (at least 0.85 of the best logged); the same seeds give a byte-identical log content hash and head hash (with a fixed clock; with the wall clock only `recorded_at` differs); every decision of a 130-step run is re-derived from the log alone and the next decision equals the replayed prediction; a run split over two calls equals one run; a flipped byte after a run fails `self_verify`.

Test floors (set after the measurement, a margin below it): learned minus random mean reward per energy > 0.2 (measured 0.40), regret versus oracle < 0.45 (measured 0.21), learned beats random in at least 15 of 20 worlds (measured 18). Guards against regression, not accuracy claims.

## Track B1: world-model learner in a menu world (synthetic world, author-defined rewards)

Everything here is the same kind of simulation as above: author-written tasks, rewards, costs and solvers, no real data. Track B asks whether a being can learn from its own log which options pay. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- menu` (2026-10-24, branch self-b1, built on commit a0ba7566).

What is new. Each step the world offers a menu of 4 tasks (domain drawn from the world seed, difficulty and listed cost and reward as before); the being picks one task and one of three solver strategies, or skips the menu for 1 energy unit. Strategies: fast (half the listed energy, exact only for difficulty 1-2, a cheap heuristic above, three times the slip rate), careful (the old scripted solver, listed energy), deep (twice the energy, exact on every template, half the slip rate). The old single-task mode and its numbers above are unchanged (the old tests still pass). The learner (`being/model.rs`, `being/planner.rs`) keeps, per (domain, difficulty, strategy), a Beta posterior of the success probability shrunk from the (domain, strategy) estimate, which is shrunk from the strategy-wide estimate (prior strength 4), plus the energy actually spent as a ratio of the listed cost. It is built only from the logged outcomes. The planner scores every (offered task, strategy) as `listed reward x min(1, p + beta x sd) / estimated energy` (UCB on the model, no random numbers, so replay is exact), takes the best affordable one, and skips when that score is below `skip_frac` times the reward per energy it has earned so far. Every decision logs all 12 alternatives with their estimates, uncertainty and scores.

Setup. Report seeds 1..20 (20 worlds), tuning seeds 101..120. Beta and skip_frac were chosen on the tuning seeds only (grid beta in 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 with skip_frac in 0, 0.3, 0.6, then beta in 1, 1.5, 2, 3 with skip_frac in 0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, at both budgets; beta 1.5 with skip_frac 1.0 had the best mean over the two budgets: 3.42 at budget 600 and 3.65 at budget 3000 on the tuning seeds, against baselines of about 1.5-2.1 there). Budgets 600 (about 150 attempts) and 3000. Baselines: random over (offer, strategy); greedy by listed reward per listed cost (uses only what is printed on the menu) with the careful strategy, and also with fast always and deep always (the best fixed strategy is the fair comparison, since the old policies cannot choose a strategy); the UCB1 domain chooser (the best old policy: UCB1 over domains, then the best listed ratio in that domain, careful); the oracle (knows the hidden success probability of every strategy and the real energy, never skips). The oracle never skips, so a learner that skips can in principle get close to or above it. Intervals are 95% t-intervals of the mean over the 20 worlds.

Verdict. The model learner beats every baseline in these worlds: +1.5 reward per energy over UCB1 at budget 600 (95% interval +1.2 to +1.8, better in 20 of 20 worlds), +1.1 over the best fixed strategy (greedy with fast, 19 of 20 worlds), and it comes within 0.38 (budget 600) and 0.16 (budget 3000, interval includes 0) of the oracle. Read this with its limits: most of the gap to UCB1 and to greedy-careful comes from choosing a strategy and from skipping, which those policies cannot do; the learner mainly found "use the fast strategy on tasks where it is reliable, skip menus where nothing looks good" (per world at budget 600: 143 fast, 11 careful, 0.3 deep attempts, 36 skips); deep is almost never worth its double energy in this world. The strategies' costs and reliabilities were written by the same author, so this shows the learner finds a good policy in this designed trade-off, not that the policy is generally good. Skipping adds a small gain (+0.17 at budget 600, 19 of 20 worlds; +0.07 at budget 3000, 15 of 20 worlds). The report-seed means are lower than the tuning-seed means (3.12 against 3.42 at budget 600), which is the usual small tuning optimism.

#### Report seeds 1..20, budget 600

| policy | mean reward per energy unit | 95% interval of the mean |
|---|---|---|
| random (offer and strategy) | 1.194 | [1.088, 1.301] |
| greedy by listed reward per cost (careful) | 1.502 | [1.336, 1.668] |
| greedy by listed reward per cost (fast always) | 2.006 | [1.626, 2.387] |
| greedy by listed reward per cost (deep always) | 1.222 | [1.132, 1.311] |
| UCB1 domain chooser (careful) | 1.593 | [1.465, 1.721] |

Calibration reading. Every prediction is made before its outcome is seen, so the points are out of sample (this is a one-step-ahead check, not a separate held-out set). The model beats the "predict the running overall success rate" baseline on Brier (0.127 against 0.169 at budget 600; 0.090 against 0.107 at budget 3000). It is overconfident where it predicts 0.2-0.6 (for example predicted 0.45, observed 0.27) and close to the diagonal from 0.6 up; the planner mostly attempts high-probability options, so the low bins hold few attempts (22-153 of 2881 at budget 600) and mostly cells with little evidence. The model's predicted success is also stored as the prediction of each attempt in the log.

Tests (`kore-self/src/being/tests.rs`, `tests/e2e_being.rs`): the menu world is deterministic and the single-task ids are unchanged; every domain has three strategies with the documented cost/reliability trade-off (deep more reliable than fast on hard templates, fast reliable on easy ones); the model folded from the log equals the live model; model.rs and planner.rs mention none of the hidden world fields (source scan); every decision of a 200-step menu run is re-derived from the log alone, with 12 logged alternatives each, and a run split over two calls equals one run; skipped menus are logged without predictions; the chooser is fixed once the being exists; a flipped byte after a model run fails verification; refill replay; the real binary runs the model chooser, explains a decision and keeps the chooser setting. Floors (a margin below the measured values at budget 600, seeds 1..20): model above UCB1 by more than 1.0 (measured 1.52), above greedy-careful and random by more than 1.0, above greedy-fast by more than 0.6 (measured 1.11), regret versus the oracle below 1.0 (measured 0.38), better than UCB1 in at least 18 of 20 worlds (measured 20), Brier below the base-rate Brier; at budget 3000 on seed 3 above UCB1 by more than 0.8. These guard against regression; they are not accuracy claims.

Not measured: worlds whose task mix or strategy trade-offs differ from this design; changing worlds (new domains appearing mid-life); strategies the learner has to discover (step B2); any language-model input (B4); the effect of the hyper-parameters outside the grid above. Changing `DEFAULT_BETA`, `DEFAULT_SKIP_FRAC` or the model's prior strength changes how an existing model-chooser log replays, so they are part of the version of the being.

## Track B2: rule discovery by verified search (synthetic world, author-defined grammar)

Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the sequence families, the grammar the search runs in, the rewards and the solvers. "Discovery" means a search inside a 17-form grammar over the being's own logged examples; it is not open-ended invention. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- discover` (2026-10-25, branch self-b2, built on commit 2d03cb28; the run takes about 6 minutes).

What is new.
* Extended pattern world (`pattern_families: extended`, default off; with it off every earlier result is bit-identical, a test checks it). Pattern tasks come from hidden families per difficulty: 1 arithmetic, 2 geometric or affine-geometric (a*t+c), 3 quadratic or cubic in n, 4 fibonacci-like or second-order recurrence (p*t[-1]+q*t[-2]) or tribonacci-like, 5 alternating add or period-3 cycle or two negative controls outside the grammar (product recurrence t[-1]*t[-2], consecutive primes). The fixed solvers know none of the new families (a test shows at most 6 of 60 tasks solved by any fixed strategy). In this world pattern tasks also pay 2x (`EXT_PATTERN_BONUS`), listed openly in every offer; without it the oracle with perfect rules gains almost nothing over the oracle with fixed solvers (see "No-bonus control").
* After every attempt the checker's exact next term is logged on the outcome event (tags `terms`, `next`). `being/discover.rs` searches only those examples. Signature = (pattern, difficulty); examples of a signature are split in log order, every third one held out. Grammar: next = sum of a_l*t[-l] over a subset of lags {1,2,3} with optional constant (14 forms) or a polynomial of degree 1-3 in the term index (3 forms); coefficients are fitted per task from its own prefix by exact rational Gauss-Jordan elimination (a rule applies only if the fit is unique, at least 3 spare equations agree exactly, coefficients are small and the next term is an integer). Smallest forms first. A form is accepted for a signature only if it is never applicable-and-wrong on training or held-out examples and reproduces at least 3 training and 1 held-out example that no smaller accepted form already explains. Accepted rules are logged as a `rule` note event plus a `rule` revision citing the example events; a fourth strategy, `discovered`, applies the being's own rule when one fits the prefix and otherwise behaves like careful; the model learner treats it as one more strategy (its estimate for that signature restarts when a rule arrives).
* Discovery runs every 10 steps of the being.

Setup. Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120, budgets 600 and 3000, beta 1.5 and skip_frac 1.0 as in B1. Chosen on the tuning seeds only: the minimum support (K_TRAIN, K_VAL), tried 4+2, 3+1, 3+2, 2+1 (recall 13%, 23%, 17%, 40% of (family, world) pairs at budget 600; precision stayed 100% for all; 3+1 chosen as a middle value, the support of only 4 examples is the weakest part of this guard), the number of spare equations (2 at first, 3 now, see below), and a curiosity bonus for pattern offers with few logged examples (0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8: it LOWERED the reward at budget 600, 3.30 / 3.13 / 2.93 / 2.70, and did not help at budget 3000, so it ships switched off). Arms, all in the extended world: random (offer and fixed strategy), the B1 model learner with fixed solvers only (it may not use `discovered`), the B1 model learner plus discovery, the oracle with fixed solvers (knows hidden success rates), the oracle with perfect rules (knows the author's rules and the hidden success rates of all four strategies). Intervals are 95% intervals of the mean over 20 worlds (t distribution).

#### No-bonus control (pattern tasks pay 1x, seeds 1..20)

Budget 3000: oracle with fixed solvers 3.418, oracle with perfect rules 3.440 (the rules are worth +0.02 in that world), no discovery 3.356, discovery 3.238 (-0.118, [-0.290, +0.054], 1 win, 5 losses, 14 ties). Recall 10.0% (12 of 120), 22 rules accepted, all exact. The being rarely attempts the harder pattern tasks when they pay little, so it logs few examples. This is why the bonus world is the main experiment, and it must be read as a world built so that the rules are worth something.

#### What was wrong at first, and the fix

The first guard needed only 2 spare equations in the prefix fit and prefixes were one term shorter. At budget 3000 (report seeds, bonus world) discovery then found 50% of the families, but 4 of 100 accepted rules were wrong: the lag-2-plus-constant rule accepted for the alternating-add family also fits a few windows of consecutive primes exactly, so it was applied to 3.1% of the prime tasks and was wrong on 9.8% of those applications (report worlds 7, 8, 10 and 20; also tuning world 119). Requiring 3 spare equations and lengthening the hidden prefixes of four families by one term removed all wrong rules (precision 100%, 0 applications to the negative families) and halved the recall, because fewer rules are applicable to short prefixes (report seeds, budget 3000: recall 50.0% with 2 spare equations, 51.7% with 3 spare equations and 3+1 support; on the tuning seeds the new guard gave 20.0% with 4+2 support and 35.0% with 3+1). The trade is real: a stricter self-check costs data.

Verdict.
* The search itself works in the sense measured here: on revealed examples alone it finds every expressible family from 8 examples, accepts nothing for the two families outside the grammar, and in the worlds it accepted 99 rules of which all 99 were exact. Replay re-derives every rule from the log alone (checked by a test and by `being_rules`).
* Whether it helps the being is not established. At budget 3000 discovery gained +0.16 reward per energy over the same learner without it (interval [+0.00, +0.32], 8 wins against 7 losses and 5 ties), about a third of the +0.49 that perfect rules would give; at budget 600 and in the no-bonus world it did not help (the point estimates are negative, intervals include 0). A tuned curiosity bonus made things worse and is off.
* Weak points. Recall is about half at budget 3000 and the median time to the first correct rule is 60 to 170 steps (60 for the simple families, 120-170 for the others); the rule for a signature needs only 4 supporting examples, validated on 1 held-out example; rules are per signature (difficulty), a rule found for one signature is not tried on another; wrong rules cannot be retired (none were accepted in the final configuration, but nothing would remove one); the chooser's estimate for `discovered` restarts when a rule arrives, and it takes tens of attempts to re-learn.

Tests (`kore-self/src/being/tests.rs`, `tests/e2e_being.rs`): the DSL evaluator on known sequences and refusals; search finds every expressible family and accepts nothing for the unexpressible ones (seeds 1..6); acceptance needs minimum support, rejects a rule that fits training but fails the held-out check, and rejects a rule that is wrong on a training example; the extended option is off by default and changes nothing when off; discovery source files name no hidden world fields; a logged discovery run stores rule revisions with cited example events and refolds to the same rule set, every rule re-derives from the examples logged before it, a second pass adds nothing; same seeds give the same log hash, two calls equal one call, a byte flip fails verify; the real binary end to end (`being_rule_discovery_end_to_end`). Floor test `measured_discovery_is_precise_finds_families_and_does_not_accept_junk` (seeds 1..6, budget 3000, measured: discovery 3.962, no discovery 3.892, random 1.133, oracle with rules 4.125, oracle fixed 3.870, 23 rules all exact, 15 of 36 families found, no application to negative families): oracle with rules at least 0.15 above oracle fixed, discovery and no discovery at least 1.5 above random, discovery not more than 0.2 below no discovery, at least 10 rules with at least 95% exact, at least 10 families found, negative-family applications at most 0.1.

Not measured: real sequences or any task not written by this author; grammars the author did not write; the algebra domain (not done); transfer of a rule between signatures; retiring a rule that later turns out wrong; more than 3000 energy per world; other values of the discovery period (5, 10 and 20 gave the same results on the first tuning grid, before the guard change); any language-model input.

## Track B3: adapting when the world changes (synthetic world, author-defined schedule)

Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the tasks, the rewards, the three scheduled changes and the learner. Question: when the world changes in the middle of the being's life, does a learner that forgets and detects changes do better than the B1 learner that keeps every observation? Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- drift` (2026-10-26, branch self-b3, built on commit f5f8be3d plus the B3 commits; about 80 s). The tuning runs are `-- drift-tune` and `-- drift-tune 2`.

What is new.
* Drifting world (`drift: true`, default off; with it off every earlier result is bit-identical, a test checks it). Three changes happen at hidden world-clock times, which scale with the being's initial budget: at about 25%, 50% and 75% of it (each moved by up to +-4% by the world seed). The being is told nothing; it sees only outcomes and the visible task features.
  1. A new domain, `units` (unit conversion, five templates, exact checker, its own hidden profile), starts to appear in the menu. It is one new feature value.
  2. A profile shift: physics pays twice as much and its difficulty mix turns easy; arithmetic becomes cheap (base cost 1). These are all visible in the listed reward and cost of the offers.
  3. The `fast` strategy degrades: its slip rate goes from 3x the domain rate to 70% (careful and deep are unchanged).
* Adaptive learner (`adapt: true`; all derived from the log only and replay-exact). (a) Cold start: a (domain, strategy) group with less than one effective attempt gets +0.25 optimism in success probability, on top of the B1 shrinkage towards the strategy-wide estimate. (b) Forgetting: every count is discounted exponentially with a half-life in attempts; the skip rule uses a discounted reward rate. (c) Change detection: for each attempt the model's own prediction for the cell is compared with the outcome before the outcome is added; the standardized residuals feed a two-sided CUSUM per (domain, strategy) (drift k = 1, threshold h = 8, started only once the cell holds 3 effective attempts). On an alarm the group's weight is cut to 10% and the change is logged as a note event plus a `belief` revision (author `rule:being-detector`) that cites the outcome events it rests on; `being_status` lists them and `being_explain` shows how many were flagged before a decision.
* The old learners stay selectable: `adapt: false` is the B1 learner, bit for bit.

Setup. Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120, budget 6000 energy units (about 2500 to 3500 steps; the changes happen after about 1500, 3000 and 4500 energy units). Compared on the same worlds: random; greedy by listed reward per cost; UCB1 over domains (B1-era baseline, which does see the new domain); the B1 model learner; B1 with exponential forgetting only (half-life 300 attempts, the best half-life for forgetting alone on the tuning seeds); B1 with the cold-start bonus only (no forgetting, detector silent), as an attribution control; the adaptive learner; and an oracle that knows the hidden success rates and the schedule (it re-optimises at the degradation; the offers it chooses from already show the new rewards and costs).

Chosen on the tuning seeds only (mean reward per energy over 20 worlds, drifting / stationary; B1 gets 4.050 / 3.656):
* Forgetting alone, by half-life in attempts: 50: 3.511 / 3.430; 100: 3.731 / 3.574; 150: 3.821 / 3.619; 300: 3.975 / 3.684; 600: 4.001 / 3.655; 1200: 4.038 / 3.661. Every half-life is at or below B1 in the drifting world.
* Forgetting + detector + cold start, grid of half-life, CUSUM (k, h), share kept and bonus: short half-lives with a sensitive detector were worse than B1 (half-life 150, k 0.5, h 4: 3.78 / 3.57 with about 10 alarms per run in both worlds, almost all false); the best cells all had a very long half-life. Chosen: half-life 5000 attempts (in a life of about 2500 attempts this is almost no forgetting; half-life 1e9 gave the same 4.141 / 3.768), k 1, h 8, keep 0.1, bonus 0.25: 4.141 drifting / 3.769 stationary, about 1.0 alarm per drifting run and 0.05 per stationary run. So the tuning itself says that forgetting does not help in this world.

| new domain appears | never (0 of 20) | 140 (19 of 20) | 150 (19 of 20) | 160 (20 of 20) |
| profile shift | never (0 of 20) | 100 (18 of 20) | 120 (19 of 20) | 100 (19 of 20) |
| fast degrades | 1170 (4 of 20) | 100 (20 of 20) | 110 (20 of 20) | 100 (20 of 20) |

New domain, from the moment it appears (energy units; median over the worlds that reached it):

| learner | until the first attempt in units | until the trailing 10 units attempts earn 80% of the oracle's rate there |
|---|---|---|
| UCB1 | 8 (20 of 20) | 892 (7 of 20) |
| B1 | 3 (20 of 20) | 142 (11 of 20) |
| forgetting only | 4 (20 of 20) | 148 (13 of 20) |
| adaptive | 3 (19 of 20) | 193 (13 of 20) |

Change detection (adaptive learner, report seeds): alarms per world 0.00 before the first change, 0.05 between the first change and the degradation, 0.75 on `fast` after the degradation (drops), 0.00 elsewhere. The degradation of `fast` was flagged in 13 of 20 worlds, median delay 265 energy units (roughly 100 steps) after the change; in the other 7 it was not flagged (the reason was not investigated). The profile shift is not a change in any success rate, only in visible rewards and costs, and no alarm was tied to it.

### Stationary world: what adaptation costs (no drift; same learners, same seeds)

| budget | adaptive minus B1 (report seeds) | forgetting only minus B1 | false alarms of the detector |
|---|---|---|---|
| 600 | -0.040 [-0.236, +0.156], 5 wins / 15 losses | -0.021 [-0.072, +0.030], 4 / 16 | 0 alarms in 20 worlds |
| 3000 | +0.047 [-0.180, +0.274], 6 / 14 | -0.046 [-0.073, -0.019], 3 / 17 | 0 alarms in 20 worlds |
| 6000 | +0.054 [-0.182, +0.290], 6 / 14 | -0.023 [-0.056, +0.010], 6 / 14 | 0 alarms in 20 worlds |

On the tuning seeds the adaptive minus B1 differences are +0.040, +0.114 and +0.113 at the three budgets and the detector raised 1 alarm in 60 worlds. Mean reward per energy of B1 / adaptive on the report seeds: 3.117 / 3.077 (600), 3.377 / 3.424 (3000), 3.395 / 3.449 (6000).

Honest reading.
* Adaptation did not help measurably in this world. The adaptive learner is 0.03 above B1 (interval -0.18 to +0.24) in the drifting world; B1 already sits within 0.08 of the oracle (interval including 0). The cold-start bonus alone gives the same (+0.038), and adding forgetting and the detector to it changes nothing (-0.008, interval -0.019 to +0.003). Wins and losses are 10 against 10, so the mean is carried by a few worlds.
* Forgetting alone hurts: in the drifting world 0 wins and 20 losses against B1 (-0.100), in the stationary world 14 to 17 losses at every budget, and every half-life on the tuning seeds was at or below B1. Discounting makes the estimates noisier, which sends the optimistic planner to re-test options it already knows.
* Why B1 is already robust here: the profile shift changes only things the offers show (listed reward and cost), which the planner reads directly each step; the new domain is handled by the shrinkage prior and the optimism of the planner (first attempt after 3 energy units); the one hidden change, the degradation of `fast`, only matters on easy tasks, where `careful` is almost as good, so an out-of-date belief costs little (B1 recovers within 100 energy units). A world where a stale belief is expensive, or where the visible features hide the change, was not tested.
* The detector does work as a detector: it flagged the degradation in 13 of 20 worlds with a median delay of 265 energy units and raised 0 false alarms in 60 stationary report worlds and 1 in 60 tuning worlds. That did not turn into reward here. At tuning time, more sensitive settings produced about 10 false alarms per run and lost reward.
* Cost in the stationary world: within noise of B1 (a difference between -0.04 and +0.05, intervals about +-0.2), but the adaptive learner lost in 14 to 15 of 20 report worlds at each budget with a positive mean at two of them. Forgetting alone costs 0.02 to 0.05.
* UCB1 over domains, which keeps cumulative averages, is far behind everything else in both worlds (about 1.9 against 3.8), so the B1 gain over it (+1.94) is the B1 result, not an adaptation result; UCB1 never recovered to 90% of the oracle after the new domain or the shift.
* The cold-start bonus (0.25) was tuned on the tuning seeds, where it gave +0.09 (drifting) and +0.11 (stationary); on the report seeds the gain is +0.04 and +0.05 with intervals crossing 0.

Test floors (`measured_adaptation_is_close_to_the_oracle_does_not_cost_much_and_detects_the_degradation`, report seeds 1..6, below the measured values): adaptive and B1 each beat UCB1 by more than 1.0; adaptive within 0.5 of the oracle; adaptive not more than 0.3 below B1 in the drifting and in the stationary world; the degradation flagged in at least 2 of the 6 worlds; at most 2 false alarms in the 6 stationary worlds. Measured on those seeds: B1 4.228, adaptive 4.201, UCB1 1.995, oracle 4.034; stationary B1 3.716, adaptive 3.712; degradation flagged in 6 of 6; no false alarm.

## Track B4: advice as an input, trust learned from outcomes (synthetic world, SIMULATED advisor)

Read this first. Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the world, the rewards, and the advisor. The advisor is a program with a quality knob `q` (with probability `q` it names the oracle-correct option, otherwise a plausible wrong one). These numbers say how a being should use advice of a GIVEN quality. They do NOT say how good any real language model is: no real model was called, the crate has no network code, and a real model's quality on real tasks is unmeasured and has to be measured separately through the command advisor (`advisor.txt`) on real tasks.

Question (the owner's): can an outside knowledge source be ONE INPUT to a mind that learns from its own experience, does it help, and how far should the being trust it? Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- advice` (menu world) and `-- advice ext` (extended pattern world), 2026-10-28, branch self-b4 on commit c6be05e3 (self-b3) plus the B4 commits. Tuning runs: `-- advice tune`, `-- advice tune-detector`. Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120 only; budgets 600 (about 154 attempts per world) and 3000 (about 723).

What is new.
* `being/advice.rs`: an `Advisor` trait; a request that carries only visible task features (domain, difficulty, listed cost and reward, strategy names, the visible terms of sequence tasks) and has no field for anything hidden; a structured reply (an option = slot + strategy, optional stated success probability; or a proposed rule of the B2 grammar). Every request, reply and what happened afterwards is a logged event (source `advisor`, ids derived from the content).
* `being/trust.rs`: trust per (advisor, domain) learned from the log. A TEST happens when the being followed advice although its own model alone preferred something else; it is won when the realized reward per energy reaches what the model alone had predicted for its own choice. Trust is the Beta(1+wins, 1+losses) posterior of the win rate. Rule proposals are factual: accepted by the verified search = win, contradicted by the being's own examples = loss, merely not yet supported = no verdict.
* Mixing (`planner.rs`): with the optimistic weight `w = clamp((mean + 1.0*sd - 0.5)/0.5, 0, 1)` the advised option's score becomes `s' = s + w*((1+0.1)*M - s)` (`M` = best own score); the best mixed score wins; the skip rule applies to it. `w = 0` is the being's own decision. The optimism is the exploration that learns trust: a new advisor is tried, and the cost of testing a useless one shrinks as 1/sqrt(tests). `trust: false` follows advice blindly (the comparison arm).
* Degradation: a one-sided CUSUM on the test residuals (k 0.5, h 6) cuts the advisor's evidence to 20% and is logged.
* Advice is never executed blindly in the trusting configuration, and a proposed rule enters the rule book only if the B2 search (training and held-out exact reproduction, never applicable-and-wrong) accepts that very form on the being's own logged examples.
* With no advisor every number is the B1 number bit for bit (a test checks it).

Arms, on the same worlds and seeds: the B1 learner without advisor; follow-advice-blindly; the trust-weighted learner; the oracle; each with simulated advisors of `q` in 0 to 1 (steps of 0.1; 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0 named), a confidently wrong advisor (`q = 0.2`, always states success probability 0.95) and an advisor that degrades from 0.9 to 0.3 at one eighth of the budget in steps (step 75 / 375).

Chosen on the tuning seeds only. Trust optimism `beta_trust` (paired mean difference of the trust arm against no advisor, averaged over q in 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0):

```
budget 600:  beta 0.5: -0.027  beta 1.0: +0.064  beta 1.5: -0.034  beta 2.0: -0.090
budget 3000: beta 0.5: -0.010  beta 1.0: +0.106  beta 1.5: +0.100  beta 2.0: +0.114
```

Chosen 1.0 (best at 600, within noise of the best at 3000; larger values test useless advisors for longer). Detector settings on the degrading advisor (tuning seeds, budget 3000): the reward is the same for every setting, including no detector at all (h = 100: +0.134 whole run, same as h 4 to 6), so the detector settings were chosen only for few false alarms: k 0.5, h 6, keep 0.2 (detected 5 of 20, 5 false alarms in 40 runs; h 4 detected 8 of 20 with 24 false alarms; k 1, h 4 detected 2 of 20 with 3).

### What the numbers say (verdict)

1. Following advice blindly is only worth it for an almost perfect advisor. Against the B1 learner without advisor, blind following loses at every `q` below about 0.93 (budget 600) / 0.97 (budget 3000): at `q = 0.9` it is 0.18 / 0.39 reward per energy worse; at `q = 0.5`, 1.31 / 1.55 worse (a loss in 19 of 20 and 20 of 20 worlds); the confidently wrong advisor costs 1.78 / 2.07. Only at `q = 1.0` (always the oracle's choice, so it plays exactly like the oracle) does it win: +0.38 [+0.11, +0.64] at 600 and +0.16 [-0.05, +0.37] at 3000. That is the break-even: roughly `q` of 0.93 to 0.97 for blind following in this world.
2. The trust learner protects against bad advice. Its paired difference against no advisor stays within noise of zero for every `q` below 0.9 (all intervals contain 0; for `q` from 0 to 0.5 it is -0.04 to +0.13), including the confidently wrong advisor (+0.01 [-0.15, +0.17] at 600, +0.07 at 3000) and the degrading one (+0.09 / +0.13 whole run, +0.00 / +0.12 after the degradation). Blind following of the same advisors loses 1.8 to 2.3. I found no `q` at which the trust arm is significantly worse than no advisor. The price of testing a useless advisor is small: for `q = 0` about 6 tests per world at 600 (3.5% of the steps, 5.7% of the energy) and 11 at 3000 (1.1%, 1.8%), the reward difference being -0.02 / +0.04 (not distinguishable from 0).
3. How much good advice helps is modest here. The B1 learner already reaches 3.377 at budget 3000 against the oracle's 3.535, so a perfect advisor can add at most 0.16. The trust learner with `q = 0.9` gains +0.15 [-0.02, +0.32] at 600 and +0.17 [-0.02, +0.36] at 3000; with `q = 1.0` +0.23 [+0.02, +0.43] and +0.20 [+0.00, +0.39] (14 and 18 wins of 20). The gain comes early in life: the median step at which the trailing 40 steps reach 90% of the oracle's rate falls from 53 to 43 (600) and from 61 to 43 (3000); in the first quarter of the run `q = 0.9` earns 2.98 against 2.74 (600), 3.38 against 3.24 (3000). Gains for `q` between 0.5 and 0.8 are positive on average (+0.05 to +0.16) but their intervals contain zero. Only `q = 1.0` has an interval that excludes zero at both budgets, and just barely at 3000. The trust learner with a perfect advisor does not reach the oracle (3.342 / 3.575 against 3.494 / 3.535 at 600; it is -0.15 [-0.30, -0.00] below blind following at 600): learning trust costs a little when the advice is perfect.
4. Calibration. The learned trust orders the advisors perfectly (rank correlation 1.00 between true `q` and learned trust over the 11 qualities, both budgets) but the level is compressed: at budget 3000 trust goes from 0.49 (`q` 0) to 0.82 (`q` 1) and the end-of-life mixing weight from 0.34 to 0.74. The reason is the definition of the test: it asks whether the followed advice beat the model's own prediction, not whether it was the oracle's choice, and a wrong option can still beat a modest prediction. So the trust is a monotone, not a calibrated, estimate of `q`, and even a useless advisor keeps a mixing weight of about 0.3 (its advice changes the choice rarely enough for this to cost little).
5. A caution on what helps. A wrong but plausible suggestion makes the being try an option it would not have tried, which is also exploration. The small positive differences at low `q` at budget 3000 (+0.04 to +0.13, all intervals contain 0) may come from that rather than from information. This experiment cannot separate the two.
6. The degradation detector contributes nothing measurable. It flagged the degradation in 1 of 20 worlds (median delay 29 steps) at 600 and in 3 of 20 (median delay 157 steps) at 3000, with no alarm before the degradation and 1 in the constant `q = 0.9` arm at 3000. The optimistic weight and the posterior already stop trusting the advisor; the reward is the same with the detector switched off on the tuning seeds.
7. Rule proposals add nothing the verified search does not already find. In the extended world every accepted rule came through the B2 acceptance (0 wrong rules in all arms, all re-derived from the log); about 4.8 proposals per world were accepted at 3000. They were not faster than discovery: the median first accepted rule is at step 46 with a `q = 0.9` advisor against step 20 for the discovery pass every 10 steps. The trust arm with `q = 0.9` and no discovery pass equals the B2 learner (+0.035 [-0.059, +0.129] at 3000, +0.198 [+0.021, +0.376] at 600, which comes from the menu advice early in life, not from the rules). Following a `q = 0.9` advisor blindly in this world loses 0.50 [-0.68, -0.32] against no advisor at 3000 and is worse than the B2 learner, because the advisor does not know the `discovered` strategy. The oracle with perfect rules stays 0.29 above the trust arm.

Honest summary: in this synthetic world advice is useful only when it is close to perfect, and even then it saves some early-life learning rather than raising the final level; a being that follows it blindly is badly hurt by anything less; a being that learns trust from its own outcomes is not hurt (no `q` where it was significantly worse) and gains a little from good advice. Whether a real model ever reaches the useful range for a real task is not known from this.

Test floors (`measured_trust_protects_against_bad_advice_and_blind_following_does_not`, report seeds 1..8, budget 600): blind following of the confidently wrong advisor is more than 1.0 below no advisor; the trust learner is within 0.5 below no advisor and more than 1.0 above blind; for `q = 0.9` the trust learner is more than 0.3 above blind following. Another test checks that blind following of a `q = 1.0` advisor reproduces the oracle's reward and energy exactly on seeds 1 to 3.

Not measured by B4: any real model; real tasks; an advisor whose errors are correlated with task difficulty or domain (`q` by domain exists in the simulated advisor but was not measured); advice in the drifting world; very long lives; other mixing formulas.

## Prediction: baseline predictors and calibration (S4; synthetic sequences, author-defined processes)

**Synthetic only.** These sequences come from `kore-self/src/predict/scenarios.rs`: four contexts, four choices, one observation per hour, with a known generating process. They say how the baselines behave when the process is exactly what the scenario describes. They say nothing about how well anything predicts a real person's choices, and no such number exists in this repository. The live ledger (`predict_make` / `predict_resolve` / `predict_score`) has not been run on real data for any period; its scoring report is only as good as the log it reads.

What is measured: a rolling-origin backtest. At each origin `t` (20 to 399) a predictor sees only observations `0..t` and the context of observation `t`, outputs probabilities over the choices seen so far plus `(other)`, and is scored on what happened. Five predictors: `uniform` (equal mass on the seen choices, 1% on `(other)`), `frequency` (smoothed counts), `last-choice` (weight `w` on the last choice, rest uniform), `recency` (counts decayed with a half-life), `context-count` (counts in this context, smoothed toward the overall frequency; refuses below 5 observations in the context). Scores: Brier (multi-class, sum of squared errors over the options, 0 best; about 0.75 for a uniform guess when 4 choices are equally likely), log loss in nats, top-label accuracy, ECE (10 equal-width bins on the top label). Intervals: moving-block bootstrap (blocks of 10, 2000 resamples, seeded) for a single run; plain bootstrap over the 20 per-seed means when averaging over seeds. Paired comparisons use the forecasts both predictors made at the same origins; the per-seed verdict is "better" only if the 95% interval of the Brier gain is above zero.

Seeds: report 1..20 (400 observations each). Parameters were chosen on seeds 101..120 only (`--tune`; mean log loss averaged over the three scenarios, one parameter at a time, the others at their defaults): `alpha` 0.1 (grid 0.1-2: log loss 1.4094-1.4166, a flat choice), `half_life` 20 (grid 5-100, best 1.3163), `last_w` 0.2 (grid 0.05-0.9, best 1.5639), `ctx_m` 5 (grid 0.5-20, 5 and 10 tie at 1.2238). The minimum-n values (10 observations; 5 in the context) are policy, not tuned.

Reproduce: `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_predict --offline --release` (about 11 s) and `... -- --tune`. Code commit `c8fcade0`, run on 2026-10-31.

### What was wrong at first

1. The first `uniform` baseline put 1/k on every option including `(other)`, which never occurs in these scenarios. Every learner then "beat" it in 20 of 20 noise seeds simply by learning that `(other)` has probability near zero (Brier gain about +0.044). That is a free win, not signal. The baseline now keeps 1% for `(other)` and shares the rest equally among seen choices; with that, no predictor beats it on noise. Numbers of the first version are not reported.
2. The first `last-choice` was parameterised as "mass spread over the others". The tuning grid's best value was at the edge and, with 3 options, gave the last choice LESS mass than the others (an anti-predictor). It is now `p = (1 - w)/k + w` on the last choice, so the last choice never gets less than any other option, and the grid was extended until an interior optimum appeared (`w` = 0.2).

### What the numbers say (verdict)

1. Context matters: context-count beats frequency and uniform in all 20 seeds. Brier 0.361 [0.283-0.414] against 0.756 and 0.750; accuracy 0.802 [0.759-0.851] against 0.245 (chance is 0.25). Paired Brier gain over frequency +0.3936 [+0.3802, +0.4081] (20 of 20 seeds better). This is the easy case by construction: each context has a favourite chosen with probability 0.8 and the overall choice frequencies are uniform, so frequency cannot see anything. It shows the machinery detects structure that is there; it does not show real choices have such structure. Coverage 0.993: context-count refused 0.7% of origins (fewer than 5 observations in the context, early in the run).
2. In the same scenario frequency, recency and last-choice give nothing: frequency is slightly WORSE than uniform (gain -0.0059 [-0.0068, -0.0049], worse in 9 seeds, no difference in 11) because it pays for estimating a distribution that is flat; recency is worse than uniform in 15 seeds; last-choice is worse than everything (Brier 0.814).
3. Pure noise: no predictor claims a win. In 0 of 20 seeds was any other predictor significantly better than uniform, and in 0 of 20 better than frequency. On average every learner is slightly worse than uniform, which is the right answer when the truth is uniform (frequency -0.0059 [-0.0066, -0.0052], recency -0.0148, context-count -0.0157 [-0.0169, -0.0142], last-choice -0.0623; the last two are worse in 17 and 20 seeds). The false-win rate of this procedure was therefore 0 of 20 seeds for the "any predictor" test; with a 95% interval per comparison a few false wins would not be surprising in other seeds.
4. Calibration on noise is near the diagonal but not on it: frequency has pooled ECE 0.0445 (confidence 0.278 against a hit rate 0.247 in the 0.2-0.3 bin; 0.325 against 0.247 in the next, so it is over-confident by 3 to 8 points); context-count has pooled ECE 0.0777 and is more over-confident, because with four contexts and 5 observations it fits chance. Uniform's per-seed ECE (median 0.020) is the floor from having only 380 forecasts per run.
5. Under context structure, context-count is under-confident: pooled ECE 0.0760, confidence 0.753 against a hit rate 0.805 in its busiest bin (smoothing toward the global frequency pulls it below the true 0.8). So it is the best predictor there but not a well calibrated one; a post-hoc recalibration was not tried.
6. Drift: recency beats frequency in all 20 seeds. Brier 0.574 [0.543-0.620] against 0.768 [0.760-0.784], gain +0.1937 [+0.1829, +0.2040]; accuracy 0.599 against 0.243; median per-seed ECE 0.040 against 0.215 for frequency, whose confidence is high exactly when the dominant choice has just changed (bin 0.4-0.5: confidence 0.443, hit rate 0.154). Recency also beats uniform (+0.1752 [+0.1656, +0.1840], 20 of 20). Frequency and context-count are worse than uniform on average here (-0.0185 and -0.0301), though no single seed shows it. The half-life (20 observations) was tuned on drift-containing mixed data on seeds 101..120 and the drift period is 100 observations; a different period would need a different half-life.
7. last-choice is metric dependent under drift: better than uniform on Brier (+0.0422 [+0.0367, +0.0469], 19 of 20 seeds) and on accuracy (0.508 against 0.230), worse on log loss (-0.0210 [-0.0318, -0.0104]), because it is confidently wrong right after each switch. It loses to recency everywhere.
8. Every predictor wins only where its assumption matches the generator (context-count with context structure, recency with drift) and none wins elsewhere; that is what the synthetic ground truth was built to show, not evidence that either assumption holds for real logs.

Caveats. All intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals, the block bootstrap is approximate, and per-seed verdicts at 95% produce about one false "better" per 20 seeds for a true tie, so single seeds should not be over-read. The generator is simple (4 choices, favourite probabilities 0.8 and 0.7, hourly steps, 400 observations); sequence length, number of choices and the strength of the structure were not varied. The choice universe is "seen so far plus `(other)`" and unseen choices are scored as `(other)`. Real logs have irregular timing, many contexts with few observations, and choices that depend on things not logged.

### What is tested (not measured)

* Leakage: for each predictor, in three scenarios and at origins 0, 9, 10, 50, 120 and 299, replacing everything after the origin by a shuffled and re-labelled future leaves every forecast up to the origin unchanged (`shuffling_future_events_does_not_change_past_predictions`); the same check run against a predictor that reads the next 20 observations reports a leak (`the_leakage_check_catches_a_predictor_that_peeks`), so the check can fail.
* Ledger: forecasts are written before any outcome exists, with the log version they were computed from (`cutoff-v<N>` in the model version); a `made_at` earlier than events already in the log is refused; `predict_resolve` refuses an outcome dated before its forecast or citing an event that is not after it; `predict_score` excludes and lists pairs written around those guards (outcome dated before the forecast, outcome in the same commit as the forecast); below the minimum number of observations a predictor does not forecast and a refusal event is logged; fewer than 30 common questions give "insufficient data", never a verdict.
* Floors (`measured_context_count_beats_frequency_where_context_matters`, `measured_no_predictor_wins_on_pure_noise`, `measured_recency_beats_frequency_under_drift`, seeds 1..8): context-count is "better" than frequency and uniform in every seed with accuracy above 0.70 and Brier below 0.5; no predictor is "better" than uniform or frequency on noise and frequency ECE stays below 0.12; recency is "better" than frequency and uniform under drift. These guard against regressions on synthetic data; they are not accuracy claims.

## Track B5: composition of verified building blocks, pruning, controller (synthetic world, author-defined families)

Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the sequence families, the 17-form grammar, the 7 transforms, the rewards and the solvers. "Composition" means a search over transform-then-form pairs where the form is one the being already accepted as a rule; it is not open-ended invention. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- b5` (modes `b5-compose`, `b5-prune`, `b5-prune-wide`, `b5-caps`, `b5-kill`, `b5-tune`), 2026-10-31, branch self-b5, commits c01c1f46 and later. Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120 (used only for the pruning settings). The model learner and its settings are those of B2 (beta 1.5, discovery pass every 10 steps); budgets 3000 and 6000.

World. `extended2` = every family of the B2 extended world plus four families outside the 17-form grammar that composition can express (a test shows the plain search never accepts them): even and odd terms following two different quadratics, n^3 plus an alternating term, a cubic plus a geometric term, and (-1)^n times a cubic; plus negative controls that nothing in the search space expresses (product recurrence, consecutive primes, a modulo-101 generator, squares modulo 7). Several families share a difficulty (one signature), so the rule for one family must never be applicable-and-wrong on the others.

### Composition vs the B2 grammar only (report seeds 1..20, n = 20 worlds)

Reward per energy unit, mean [95% interval of the mean]:

| policy | budget 3000 | budget 6000 |
|---|---|---|
| no discovery | 3.654 [3.297, 4.010] | 3.722 [3.374, 4.069] |
| B2 discovery (17-form grammar only) | 3.648 [3.291, 4.005] | 3.721 [3.374, 4.068] |
| discovery with composition | 3.654 [3.301, 4.007] | 3.736 [3.398, 4.074] |

Paired differences: composition minus grammar only +0.006 [-0.008, +0.019] (2 wins, 1 loss, 17 ties) at 3000 and +0.015 [-0.023, +0.053] (2 wins, 2 losses, 16 ties) at 6000. Grammar only minus no discovery -0.006 [-0.014, +0.002] and -0.001 [-0.004, +0.003]. Composition minus no discovery -0.000 [-0.016, +0.015] and +0.014 [-0.023, +0.052]. **No reward gain from composition is established in this world.** Rules answer very few attempts (per world: B2 3.4 and 5.4, composition 5.2 and 14.4 of about 700 and 1400 attempts), so even a larger rule book changes little.

What composition does change is what gets found. Families covered by the final rule book (at least 90% exact on 100 fresh tasks of the family, scored against hidden truth that the being never sees), worlds out of 20, budget 3000 / 6000:

| family | B2 grammar only | composition |
|---|---|---|
| even/odd quadratics (parity split) | 0 / 0 | 9 / 9 |
| n^3 + alternating term | 0 / 0 | 5 / 6 |
| cubic + geometric (second differences) | 0 / 0 | 4 / 4 |
| (-1)^n times a cubic | 0 / 0 | 2 / 2 |
| the six B2 grammar families, summed over families | 32 / 35 of 120 | 35 / 38 of 120 |

Recall of the composable families: 0 of 80 for B2, 20 of 80 (25.0%) at 3000 and 21 of 80 (26.2%) at 6000 for composition. Recall is low: a block must be accepted first (for example the cubic polynomial from another family), and families that share a signature dilute each other's examples, as in B2. Composed rules accepted over all 20 worlds at 3000: parity then difference then polynomial 1: 9; parity then polynomial 3: 7; second differences then a 3-lag recurrence: 5; second differences then lag-2 with constant: 2.

Junk or wrong rules. Rules accepted: B2 55 and 59, composition 81 and 87 (23 and 24 composed). Exact on 300 fresh tasks of their signature (never applicable-and-wrong, right at least once): all of them. Wrong or overfit: **0** in every arm, worlds with a wrong rule 0 of 20. Negative controls on fresh tasks with the final book: for all four families, in both arms, the share of tasks where some rule was applied is 0.000 and the wrong share is 0.000. Separately, tests run the search on 200 examples of each negative control in 10 worlds with nine blocks supplied: 0 rules accepted.

### Pruning, rule drift (report seeds 1..20)

Settings chosen on tuning seeds 101..120 at budget 3000: window 6 latest uses, at least 4 uses, retire below a 0.5 success rate (grid tried: (10,6,0.5), (10,6,0.3), (8,5,0.5), (10,8,0.5), (16,8,0.4), (6,4,0.5); wrong rule answers after the change per affected world 2.17, 2.50, 2.00, 2.17, 2.83, 1.83 against 3.50 without pruning; reward per energy identical to 0.003; no retirements in the stationary control for any setting). The planned 7th setting and the budget 6000 grid were not run (my run hit its time limit). A rule is also merged into a simpler live rule of the same signature when it applies to at least 5 logged examples and the simpler rule always agrees.

Narrow drift: at half the budget the revealed next term of one family (difficulty 2, affine-geometric) changes, so the old rule fits every prefix and gives a wrong answer. Worlds where that rule was live at the change: 9 of 20. Over those worlds, after the change, budget 3000, no cap:

| measure | no pruning | pruning |
|---|---|---|
| wrong answers produced by a rule, per world | 0.222 | 0.222 |
| reward per energy | 3.691 | 3.691 |

Identical: the being almost never used the stale rule (7.9 rule answers per world, 2 wrong in total) because its world model had already learned that the `discovered` strategy fails there. With a live-rule cap of 8: wrong answers 0.556 vs 0.333 per world (difference -0.222 [-0.687, +0.243], lower in 1 of 9 worlds), one retirement. Budget 6000, no cap: 0.444 vs 0.444, reward 3.709 vs 3.707.

Wide drift (four families with plain rules change at half the budget; measurement-only world option), budget 3000, 11 of 20 worlds with a stale rule live, no cap:

| measure | no pruning | pruning |
|---|---|---|
| wrong answers produced by a rule, per world | 2.455 | 1.182 (difference -1.273 [-3.937, +1.391]; lower in 1 of 11 worlds) |
| share of rule answers that are wrong (pooled) | 0.500 | 0.361 |
| reward per energy | 3.667 | 3.668 (+0.002 [-0.002, +0.005]) |

Retirements in the pruning arm: 4 (3 low success, 1 merged), in 1 world with a retirement after the change (first one 47 steps after the change). **Wrong-rule use falls in the wide scenario, but the effect rests on one world and its interval includes zero; there is no reward effect.** Stationary control (no drift): reward identical with and without pruning (3.654); 2 merges in 20 worlds, no low-success retirement, so pruning did not remove good rules here.

Rule count over time (mean live rules over 20 worlds, no cap, narrow scenario, no pruning vs pruning): after step 25: 0.40 / 0.40, 100: 1.00 / 1.00, 200: 2.25 / 2.25, 300: 3.35 / 3.30, 400: 3.85 / 3.75, 600: 4.00 / 3.90 (wide: 3.70 / 3.55 at 400). Without a cap the largest rule count in any world was 15 (narrow, no pruning) and 13 with pruning; with a cap of 8 the largest was 8, with 6 cap refusals logged per arm.

### Caps and kill switch

Caps run (budget 3000, 20 worlds, composition on): live rules 3, building blocks 2, search candidates per pass 60, steps per run 400, energy per run 900. Largest value seen: live rules 3, blocks used 2, candidates per pass 60, steps 400: **no cap exceeded**. Energy: the cap stops new steps once reached; overshoot was at most 4 units (a step that starts below the cap may end above it). 19 of 20 runs ended at the energy cap, 1 at the step limit. Refusals recorded: search candidates 47, live rules 3, building blocks 4; in a logged run each is a `controller_refusal` event (tests compare counts with the log).

Kill switch: a check turned on before step 41 stopped 20 of 20 runs after exactly 40 steps. Tests also cover a KILL file present at the start (refused and audited), a KILL file created while the loop runs (the next check stops it: 7 steps ran, the file appeared at the 8th check) and the stop event in the log.

### What is tested (not measured)

controller.txt parsing (defaults, hard maxima, unknown or repeated keys, fail closed: every cap 0), the reserved-file refusal for every spelling of `controller.txt`, audit rows for each refusal kind, replay of composed and retired rules from the log alone (rule re-derivation includes composed rules), time travel across a retirement, nothing deleted, a capped search being a prefix of the uncapped search, the source scans (the being sources have no file or network API; `discover.rs` names no hidden family).

### What B5 does not show

No reward gain from composition; the pruning effect is small and rests on a few worlds; the families, transforms and rewards are the author's; the tuning grid was cut short; no real data, no real language model, no long unattended run, no crash recovery; sensitivity to the world design (the number of families sharing a signature, prefix length) was not swept.

## Track B6: transfer between domains (synthetic world, author-defined families)

Everything here is a simulation written by one author: the two phases of the world, the hidden value map, the families, the rewards, the solvers and the learner. "Transfer" means two specific things: (1) the cells of a new domain start from the posterior of the same (difficulty, strategy) cell of a learned domain, chosen by a similarity read from logged outcomes, with a guard that can switch the link off; (2) the rule search tries rules already accepted in the other domain first. Measured with `cargo run -p kore-self --example measure_being --offline --release -- b6` (also `b6 6000`, `b6-tune`, `b6-tune-guard`), 2026-10-31, branch self-b6 (built on self-b5 a79f7f31). Report seeds 1..20, tuning seeds 101..120 (used only for the settings below). Budgets 3000 (main) and 6000. Discovery pass every 10 steps, composition on, B5 learner (beta 1.5) in every arm.

World (`transfer: true`, needs extended2, default off; a test shows every earlier result is bit for bit unchanged). A life has two phases. Phase 1 (about the first 40% of the budget, moved by +-3% by the world seed, hidden) offers only sequence tasks, domain A (the extended2 families). From then on the offers are drawn from three domains: A again, B (`pattern_b`: the same families, but every term and the revealed next term are passed through a hidden affine map a*v+b with a in {2,3}, b in 1..9) and a control domain C (unit conversions, no sequence structure). B shares building blocks with A and is not identical: polynomial forms carry over unchanged, but recurrences without a constant term (geometric, Fibonacci-like, tribonacci-like) need a constant term in B, and the fixed solvers that were exact on A for geometric and Fibonacci-like sequences are no longer exact on B. B and A pay like each other (copied hidden profile, 2x pattern bonus); C pays like the units domain. B's rules are their own (signature = difficulty + 10), found on B's own revealed examples.

Mechanism (log-derived only, replay-exact). Similarity (`being/transfer.rs`): for the logged examples of B, the share on which the first applicable rule of A at the same difficulty (accepted in A after the full B2/B5 verification), or the same rule with its constant term toggled, gives the exact next term, pooled over difficulties; a link needs at least 3 examples, at least 2 right, no wrong application and a share of at least tau. Then every difficulty at which A's cell holds at least 4 effective attempts is linked. A linked cell takes the source cell's posterior as its prior (weight XFER_K pseudo-observations) in place of the strategy-wide chain; the `discovered` strategy of B is linked only once B has a live rule at that difficulty. Guard (`model.rs`): after at least 4 attempts a link influenced, if the observed outcomes are less likely under the transferred prior than under the plain prior by more than 2 nats of log-likelihood, the link is switched off for good. Every link and every revocation is a note plus a revision of `being/transfer/NNNN` citing the logged examples or attempts it rests on; links are read back from the log on replay, revocations are re-derived by the fold; a test checks that the replayed model equals the live one. The rule search under transfer: A's accepted rules (and constant-toggled forms) are tried first for the same difficulty in B; acceptance is unchanged (3 training and 1 held-out new exact reproductions, 3 spare equations, never applicable-and-wrong), so only the order of trial changes.

Settings, chosen on tuning seeds 101..120 only. tau 0.34 / 0.5 / 0.67 with XFER_K 4 / 8 / 16 (transfer minus no transfer, first 100 steps after B appears, reward per energy): tau 0.34: +0.183, +0.202, +0.215; tau 0.5: +0.181, +0.199, +0.213; tau 0.67: +0.050, +0.050, +0.053 (the 0.67 rows link in fewer worlds; the 0.34 and 0.5 rows differ by less than 0.005 and every interval overlaps). Chosen: tau 0.5, XFER_K 16. Guard threshold 0.5 / 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 nats (shifted-cells control, guard on minus guard off, first 100 steps): +0.235, +0.235, +0.232, +0.221, +0.199, all with 9 or 10 wins and 0 losses of 20; the right-source links the guard wrongly revoked per world: 0.15, 0.15, 0.00, 0.00, 0.00. Chosen: 2 nats (no false revocation on the tuning seeds, almost the same protection). The planned discovery-order switch was not tuned (it has no setting).

Arms on identical worlds (same world seed, same tasks): no transfer (the B5 learner); transfer (links, guard, search order); links only (transfer without the changed search order); three controls that use the same trigger as the transfer arm but the wrong source: "right domain, shifted cells" (the sequence domain A is the right source, but each difficulty borrows the cell of the next difficulty, cyclic), guard on and off, and "wrong similarity" (B linked to the most dissimilar learned domain other than A, C linked to the most dissimilar learned domain, by distance between pooled success rates of the fixed strategies), guard on and off; and an oracle (knows the hidden success rates, holds rules found with 150 examples per domain and difficulty). The controls exist to show what bad transfer would cost; the tools cannot switch them on.
